strengths: The paper proposes a clear and original idea: designing per-instance diffusion noise schedules from the image power spectrum, rather than using a fixed global schedule or resolution-dependent heuristic. This is a meaningful conceptual contribution for pixel-space diffusion.

The method is technically well motivated. The RAPSD-based derivation connects noise levels to frequency-dependent signal destruction, and the paper gives concrete closed-form schedules, training and sampling algorithms, and a simple conditional spectrum sampler for inference.

The empirical evaluation is strong within the stated scope. The authors reproduce the SiD2 baseline and compare against recent single-stage pixel diffusion methods on ImageNet at 128, 256, and 512 resolution. The gains are most convincing in the low-NFE regime, where the proposed schedules substantially reduce FID degradation.

The ablations are useful and targeted. The paper tests fixed median schedules, cosine schedules with spectral min/max, frequency-only and power-only schedules, additional conditioning, logSNR versus t-based guidance intervals, and an oracle ground-truth spectrum condition. These ablations support the main design decisions.

Presentation is generally clear. The paper explains the connection between spectrum, resolution, and noise schedules well, and the limitations section honestly notes that the method still lags latent diffusion and distilled models and that some hyperparameters remain tuned manually.
weaknesses: The theoretical claims are somewhat stronger than the derivations justify. The 'bounds' on minimum and maximum noise are based on expected RAPSD, power-law and monotonic-spectrum assumptions, and approximations such as Ψ(1) >> 1 and Ψ(Nf) << 1. These are useful heuristics, but not rigorous guarantees for arbitrary images or generated samples.

The scope of evidence is narrow: all main results are class-conditional ImageNet pixel diffusion based on a SiD2-style architecture. The paper does not demonstrate transfer to text-to-image, unconditional generation, non-natural-image domains, video, latent diffusion, rectified flows, or distilled samplers, even though some of these are discussed as motivating contexts.

The practical advantage is partly entangled with additional tuning. The method introduces κmin, κmax, t-based guidance intervals, extra FiLM conditioning, and a learned RAPSD sampler; several are resolution-dependent or separately tuned. This weakens the claim that the approach removes manual schedule tuning entirely.

The per-instance benefit is real but not isolated as dramatically as the headline suggests. The fixed median spectral schedule already improves over SiD2, so part of the gain may come from a better global spectral schedule rather than per-instance adaptation; the incremental benefit over the fixed spectral schedule should be discussed more carefully.

The paper does not report training compute, wall-clock overhead, RAPSD computation overhead, or training-seed variability. Metrics are averaged over five generation seeds, but it is unclear whether model training was repeated. Reproducibility would be stronger with code, exact training budgets, and implementation details for all baselines.

The method slightly worsens at high denoising-step counts, which is acknowledged but not deeply explained. This matters because it suggests the 'tight' schedules trade off asymptotic sampling quality for low-step efficiency.

Ethics and broader impacts are not substantively discussed. The work is mainly methodological, but image generation models can inherit dataset biases and misuse risks, so a short treatment would be appropriate.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete weakness of standard pixel-diffusion noise schedules and proposes an intuitively motivated per-instance alternative based on image spectra.
The experimental section includes strong ImageNet-scale comparisons to a close baseline, SiD2, across 128, 256, and 512 resolutions, with consistent FID gains and especially better low-NFE behavior.
Ablations are useful: the paper separates the effects of the fixed median schedule, min/max conditioning, guidance interval parameterization, and the sampled-vs-oracle spectrum mechanism.
The presentation is generally clear, with algorithms, closed-form schedule derivations, implementation details, and hyperparameter tables that make the method understandable.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claims are weaker than presented. The min/max noise arguments rely on idealized assumptions such as monotone power-law spectra, expected white-noise RAPSD, and heuristic tolerance constants; these do not constitute strong bounds on generative performance or schedule optimality.

The best schedule is an ad hoc average of frequency-focused and power-focused schedules, while either component alone performs very poorly. This raises concern that the proposed principle is incomplete and that performance depends on empirical tuning rather than the claimed spectral derivation.

The empirical scope is narrow: results are only for class-conditional ImageNet pixel diffusion. The paper does not demonstrate usefulness for text conditioning, latent diffusion, video, non-natural-image data, or distilled/flow models, despite positioning the idea broadly.

The fairest gains over SiD2 are meaningful but not decisive in all settings: improvements are small for the heavy model and at 128 resolution, and the method still lags stronger latent or distilled systems. The claimed significance is therefore limited to a specialized pixel-diffusion regime.

Efficiency is evaluated mainly by NFE, but the method adds per-instance schedule computation, extra conditioning, a learned RAPSD sampler, and additional hyperparameter tuning. Wall-clock sampling/training cost and memory overhead are not reported, weakening the low-step efficiency claim.

Reproducibility is only moderate. The paper gives many details, but no code or trained model release is described, and reproducing ImageNet-scale runs with 5 seeds is expensive. Some important choices, such as loss bias tuning and guidance intervals across resolutions, remain hand-tuned.

The limitations section is honest but incomplete: it notes limited applicability and tuning needs, but does not fully discuss failure modes when the sampled spectrum is wrong, robustness outside ImageNet, or potential bias introduced by class-conditional spectral priors.

strengths: Soundness: The method is technically well motivated: the paper derives how noising affects the radially averaged power spectral density, uses this to set per-instance minimum/maximum noise levels, and builds frequency-focused, power-focused, and mixed schedules. The derivations are simple but appropriate for the claimed schedule design.

Empirical evidence is strong for the main setting. On ImageNet 128/256/512, the proposed schedules improve over a carefully reproduced SiD2 baseline, often with substantially fewer denoising steps; the low-step regime results are especially convincing.

The fairest comparison is well handled: the authors keep the SiD2 architecture and training protocol mostly fixed, reproduce SiD2, report multiple metrics, and average their main results over five generation seeds.

The ablations are useful and directly probe the design: median fixed schedule, cosine min/max, frequency-only, power-only, conditioning removal, logSNR interval guidance, and oracle ground-truth spectrum. These support the claim that the mixed per-instance schedule and extra conditioning matter.

Significance: The contribution is meaningful for single-stage pixel diffusion, where sampling efficiency remains a real bottleneck. A schedule-level improvement that reduces NFE without distillation or latent autoencoders is practically useful and complementary to other advances.

Originality: Per-instance spectral noise schedules are a fresh and elegant extension of prior work on resolution-dependent schedules and spectral interpretations of diffusion. The paper connects natural-image spectra to schedule construction in a clean way.

Presentation is generally clear, with algorithms, equations, figures, tables, and implementation details that make the method understandable. The limitations section is honest about lagging behind latent/distilled models and the remaining need to tune loss bias and guidance intervals.
weaknesses: The evaluation is narrow: all main experiments are class-conditional ImageNet generation. The paper would be stronger with at least one additional dataset or text-conditional setting to show that the gains are not ImageNet-specific or tied to class-label spectrum statistics.

The method introduces new hyperparameters and tuning decisions, including kappa_min, kappa_max, the mixed schedule choice, loss bias, and t-based guidance intervals. Although ablations are provided, the claim of resolution adaptation without hyperparameter changes is partly weakened because other settings still require tuning across resolutions/models.

The theoretical analysis relies on simplifying assumptions: variance-preserving schedules, monotone power-law RAPSD approximations, and expected white-noise spectra. These are reasonable, but the paper does not deeply analyze when the approximation breaks down, e.g. images with unusual spectra, non-natural images, or latent representations.

The reported gains over the strongest SiD2 flop-heavy baseline are modest at some resolutions, especially at 128x128 where FID is tied and IS is worse. The contribution is still useful, but not uniformly large across compute regimes.

Reproducibility is decent in the manuscript, but exact reproduction would depend on releasing code, trained models, exact evaluation scripts, generated sample seeds, and details of the SiD2 reproduction. The paper describes many settings but does not by itself guarantee full reproducibility.

The paper has little explicit discussion of research ethics or evaluation cost. For an image generation paper, it should briefly address dataset licensing/provenance, misuse considerations, and the compute/API/environmental cost of large-scale ImageNet training and evaluation.

The comparison excludes latent diffusion and distilled models for understandable reasons, but this means the practical state-of-the-art relevance is somewhat bounded: the method is best viewed as an advance within single-stage pixel diffusion rather than as a new overall image-generation frontier.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful idea: adapting diffusion noise schedules to per-instance spectral statistics, with a simple two-parameter power-law RAPSD representation and a lightweight sampler for generation time.

The methodology is mostly sound. The derivation connecting noised RAPSD to appropriate minimum/maximum noise levels is plausible, and the final schedule is implemented with modest changes to an existing strong pixel-diffusion baseline.

The empirical evaluation is strong for the main claim. The authors reproduce SiD2, compare across ImageNet 128/256/512, report multiple metrics, average key results over 5 generation seeds, and show consistent gains especially in the low-NFE regime.

Ablations are useful: fixed median schedules, cosine min/max schedules, frequency-only and power-only schedules, removal of min/max conditioning, logSNR guidance intervals, and oracle spectra help isolate why the mixed per-instance schedule matters.

The paper is well written and well organized, with clear algorithms, implementation details, extra high-NFE analysis, computational cost discussion, and an honest limitations section noting that the method still lags latent/distilled models and requires tuning of loss bias/guidance intervals.
weaknesses: The final mixed schedule is partly heuristic. The spectral bounds motivate the endpoints, but the average of frequency-focused and power-focused schedules is selected empirically; the theoretical story does not fully justify why this particular interpolation should be optimal or robust.

The inference-time method is only indirectly per-instance: the actual image spectrum is unavailable and is sampled from a conditional GMM. This weakens the central framing somewhat, especially for text-to-image where the oracle spectrum is substantially better, suggesting spectrum prediction/distribution shift is a real bottleneck.

The comparison is strongest against SiD2-style single-stage pixel diffusion, but the practical significance is narrower because the method remains behind strong latent diffusion and distilled models in quality/step efficiency. The contribution is therefore most compelling as an improvement within a specialized regime.

Some experimental details needed for full reproducibility are missing or underspecified, including code availability, exact large-scale training compute for the main diffusion models, full dataset details for the text-to-image training set, and confidence intervals or variance for many reported metrics beyond the averaged SiD2/ours ImageNet results.

The method introduces additional tuning choices despite claiming reduced schedule handcrafting: kappa values, guidance intervals, loss bias, and NFE optima are still selected per setting in practice. The paper acknowledges part of this, but it reduces the strength of the resolution/dataset generality claim.

The impact statement is boilerplate and does not meaningfully discuss risks specific to improved image generation, such as misuse, dataset bias, or provenance concerns. There are no obvious unresolved ethical blockers, but the treatment is shallow.

strengths: The paper studies an important practical bottleneck for single-stage pixel diffusion: the large number of denoising steps needed relative to latent diffusion. A per-instance schedule based on image spectra is a plausible and potentially useful direction.

The manuscript gives a clear high-level derivation connecting the expected RAPSD of a noised image to the signal spectrum, and it provides a concrete training and sampling procedure rather than only an analysis.

The evaluation includes reasonably strong pixel-diffusion baselines, multiple ImageNet resolutions, several metrics, low-NFE curves, text-to-image results, and ablations over schedule design, conditioning, guidance interval, and spectrum sampling.
The authors are fairly explicit about some limitations: the method still lags behind latent/distilled models, requires tuning other hyperparameters, and exhibits degradation at high step counts.
weaknesses: The central theoretical story is weaker than the paper suggests. The derivation only justifies expected RAPSD under Gaussian noise and heuristic choices of minimum/maximum tolerances; it does not establish that the resulting schedule is optimal or even reliably better for the diffusion training objective. The final mixed schedule is an empirical average of two schedules whose individual ablations perform very poorly, so the claimed principled design is only partially supported.

The empirical gains are more modest and more confounded than the framing implies. A fixed median spectral schedule already recovers much of the improvement over SiD2, suggesting that the per-instance component may be smaller than advertised. The method also changes conditioning and guidance interval definitions, and the paper does not fully isolate whether the baseline would improve under the same retuning.

The strongest claims are limited to single-stage pixel diffusion, a specialized setting that the paper acknowledges is not competitive with latent diffusion or distilled models. This reduces significance despite useful improvements in that niche.

The high-step degradation is concerning. The method is advertised as a tighter and more efficient schedule, but FID worsens at larger NFEs, especially for stronger/easier settings and text-to-image. The proposed explanation as diversity loss is plausible but not fully resolved, and it raises questions about robustness of the schedule/sampler mismatch.

The text-to-image evaluation is not very reproducible or cleanly comparable. The training dataset is described only indirectly as the same as SiD2, SiD2 implementation details were not available, and the authors' reproduction already beats the reported SiD2 numbers before applying the proposed method. This makes it hard to attribute the reported gap to the proposed schedule.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for an ICML main-track paper at this scale. The appendix gives some sampler and hyperparameter details, but does not provide enough information about full diffusion training compute, optimizer schedules, dataset preprocessing, exact evaluation protocol variants, or code/model availability for independent reproduction.

The limitations and ethics treatment are inadequate. The impact statement is essentially boilerplate and dismisses potential societal consequences of improving image generation without discussing misuse, dataset issues, or deployment risks.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful idea: designing per-instance diffusion noise schedules from image spectral statistics, with a simple RAPSD power-law approximation and a lightweight sampler for inference-time schedules.

The empirical evidence is convincing for the intended setting of single-stage pixel diffusion. The authors reproduce SiD2, compare at 128/256/512 ImageNet resolutions, report multiple metrics, average key results over five generation seeds, and show especially strong gains in the low-NFE regime.

Ablations are strong and targeted: fixed median schedules, cosine min/max schedules, frequency-only and power-only schedules, min/max conditioning, guidance interval choices, oracle spectra, and hyperparameter sweeps all help isolate where the gains come from.
The method is practically attractive: the RAPSD sampler is small, the added inference overhead is negligible, and the best models use substantially fewer denoising steps than the SiD2 baseline.

The paper is well written and honest about limitations: it notes that the method still lags latent/distilled models, that some hyperparameters still require tuning, and that high-NFE sampling can degrade diversity.
weaknesses: The theoretical development motivates the schedule but remains partly heuristic. In particular, the mixed frequency/power schedule and the choice of kappa bounds are empirically selected rather than derived from an optimization objective tied directly to likelihood or sample quality.

The scope is somewhat narrow: the strongest claims are demonstrated mainly for single-stage pixel diffusion, while the paper explicitly does not establish whether the approach transfers to latent diffusion, distilled models, rectified flows, or video generation.

The text-to-image results are promising but less conclusive. The oracle spectrum gap on MS-COCO suggests that the RAPSD sampler can suffer under train-test distribution shift, and the training dataset/details for the reproduced text-to-image setup are not described as fully as the ImageNet setting.
Some improvements require per-resolution guidance interval and NFE tuning, which weakens the claim that the schedule broadly removes manual tuning, even though kappa values themselves are shared.

The high-NFE degradation/diversity issue is investigated thoughtfully, but it remains an unresolved behavior of the proposed tight schedules and complicates deployment when the optimal step count is unknown.

Reproducibility is adequate in terms of algorithms, hyperparameters, metrics, and compute discussion, but the manuscript does not appear to include a code release or enough low-level training details to make exact reproduction easy at this scale. The ethics statement is very generic for image generation work and does not discuss misuse or dataset concerns.
